description_full: HNI Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture, sale, and marketing of workplace furnishings and residential building products primarily in the United States and Canada. The company operates in two segments, Workplace Furnishings and Residential Building Products. The Workplace Furnishings segment offers panel-based and freestanding furniture systems, seating, benching, tables, architectural products, storage, ancillary products, hospitality products, and social collaborative items through a system of independent dealers, company-owned dealers, and office product distributors, as well as directly to end-user customers and governments. The Residential Building Products segment provides various gas, wood, electric, and pellet-fueled fireplaces; and inserts, stoves, facings, outdoor fire pits and fire tables, and accessories through independent dealers and distributors, as well as corporation-owned installing distribution and retail outlets. It sells its products under the Allsteel, AMQ, Beyond, Coalesse, D'style, David Edward, Designtex, Gunlocke, HALCON, HBF, HBF Textiles, HON, Interwoven, Kimball, Kimball Hospitality, National, Orangebox, Smith System, Steelcase, and Viccarbe brand names. The company was incorporated in 1944 and is headquartered in Muscatine, Iowa.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 18K people. Revenue per employee of $153K ranks in the bottom quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $11K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $1K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 20× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: HNI Corporation is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.4B market cap on $2.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 10% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 36%.

The business throws off $208M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.10× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.6× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 5.0×.
Shareholder yield of 4.2% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.54x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 22% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 36% and a beta of 0.93, it moves roughly with the market.
About $24.0M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 55% in the 2020 crash, 39% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 9% below its DCF fair value of $51.93, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 49%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $33.62 to $79.59 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Consumer Cyclical peers: cheaper on EV/EBITDA 8.9 vs 11.2, richer on P/E 157.5 vs 19.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 22% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 6.1% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.5% (vs the 8% bar).
The 4 covering analysts target $71.00 on average, 50% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 10% earns above the cost of capital of 7.8%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.34).
It runs a 36% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 3% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.6x net debt to EBITDA ($215.7M of cash against $1.3B of debt), with interest covered 5.0x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.57 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 6.3% over 3 years, 7.7% over 5 years and 2.1% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 9.6% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 3.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.6x depreciation (2.4% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.1%, and institutions hold 89%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $4.6M sold).
It returns 4.2% a year to shareholders (2.3% in buybacks and 3.0% in dividends).
The share count has grown 10.8% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 460% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 18,500 employees, each generates about $153K of revenue, 0.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 3.5% a year.
That works out to $11K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $3.1M (20x revenue per employee).
